Work and Vocation
wurk and voh-KAY-shun
noun phrase (the doctrine of calling)
From “work” and “vocation” (Latin vocatio, a calling); the doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, to be done heartily as unto the Lord.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Work and vocation name the doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, instituted at creation and to be done heartily as unto the Lord. Work is not a result of the fall but a creation ordinance: before sin entered, “the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.” The fall brought toil, sweat, and thorns, but did not make labour itself a curse; work remains a creational good and a calling. The apostle dignifies all lawful labour by directing it to God: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men”; and he lays down the plain rule against idleness, “that if any would not work, neither should he eat,” and bids every man “abide in the same calling wherein he was called.” The dictionary marks the doctrine of vocation as the Reformation's great recovery against the medieval notion that only the priest, monk, and nun had a “calling,” while ordinary labour was a lower, secular thing. The Reformers taught that the farmer, the mother, the merchant, and the magistrate serve God in their callings as truly as the minister—that there is no sacred-secular divide, and that the milkmaid milking her cow to the glory of God does a work as holy as the preacher in his pulpit. The dictionary holds this against two errors: the false spirituality that despises ordinary work as unspiritual, and the modern idolatry of work that makes career the source of identity and worth, the idol of the heart before which the age bows. True vocation is neither despised nor idolized: it is honest labour received as a calling from God, done diligently and heartily to His glory, balanced by the Sabbath rest He appointed, and held as service to God and neighbour, not as the ground of one's worth.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, instituted at creation and done heartily as unto the Lord (Genesis 2:15; Colossians 3:23); the Reformation's recovery against the sacred-secular divide, against both despising work and idolizing career.

WORK AND VOCATION, noun phrase. [Latin vocatio, a calling.] Honest labour as a God-given calling.

Work is a creation ordinance: man put in the garden to dress and keep it (Genesis 2:15).

“Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Colossians 3:23).

Against idleness: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

The Reformation's recovery against the sacred-secular divide in callings.

📖 Key Scripture

Ge 2:15 — "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it."

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

1 Co 7:20 — "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called."

2 Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

One error is the false spirituality that despises ordinary work as unspiritual; the other is the modern idolatry of work that makes career the source of identity and worth—the idol of the heart of the age.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of honest labour as a calling from God. The first corruption is the false spirituality, ancient and modern, that despises ordinary work as unspiritual—ranking the “sacred” callings of ministry above the “secular” labour of the farmer, the mother, and the merchant. The Reformation recovered the truth against this: there is no sacred-secular divide in callings; the believer serves God in his lawful work as truly as the minister in his, and the humblest labour done heartily to the Lord is holy. Work is a creation ordinance, given before the fall, a good and dignified service to God and neighbour.

The opposite and more modern corruption is the idolatry of work—making career the source of identity, meaning, and worth, the idol of the heart before which the age bows. The man who finds his whole self in his work has made a god of it, and when the work fails he is undone. The dictionary holds the balance: work is neither to be despised nor idolized. It is honest labour received as a calling from God, done diligently and heartily to His glory, balanced by the Sabbath rest He appointed, and held as service rendered to God and neighbour—never as the ground of one's worth, which rests in being made in God's image and, for the believer, redeemed by Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin vocatio (a calling) and “work”; the doctrine that labour is a creation ordinance and a divine calling, recovered by the Reformers against the sacred-secular divide.

Vocatio, Latin, a calling, the root of “vocation.”

Work as a creation ordinance, given before the fall (Genesis 2:15).

Done “heartily, as to the Lord” (Colossians 3:23).

The Reformation's recovery: every lawful calling serves God.

Balanced by the Sabbath rest, against the idolatry of work.

Usage

"The pastor preached vocation: the believer serves God in his work as truly as the minister."

"He honoured ordinary labour as a calling, against the divide of sacred and secular."

"She warned against the idolatry of career, the modern idol of the heart."
